claims.text: Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower thermal stability than larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles under comparable heating conditions.
The onset temperature for significant structural evolution will be lower in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are equiatomic.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are single-phase.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have minimal surface segregation.
Classical molecular dynamics can be used to investigate the thermal response of HEA nanoparticles.
Validated interatomic potentials are available for classical molecular-dynamics modeling of the specified FeCuCrCoNi system.
Nanoparticles of different sizes will be subjected to a common temperature ramp in the proposed simulations.
The simulations will use vacuum-like conditions and a fixed linear heating rate.
Particle size determines the nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio.
Surface-to-volume ratio influences surface atomic coordination and diffusion dynamics.
Smaller nanoparticles have stronger surface effects, including higher surface energy and greater atomic mobility.
Enhanced surface atomic mobility can promote surface reconstruction or phase separation during heating.
Premature surface reconstruction or phase separation reduces the thermal stability of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The critical temperature for melting or phase rearrangement will decrease systematically as nanoparticle size decreases.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles behave more like bulk material and therefore undergo structural evolution at higher temperatures.
Heating rate, environmental pressure, and interatomic-potential accuracy may alter the predicted size-dependent response.
Radial distribution functions, coordination numbers, and mean-square displacements can be monitored to identify structural changes during simulated heating.
The hypothesis is falsified if smaller nanoparticles do not consistently have lower structural-change onset temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
